unit.title: Subjunctive in Relative Clauses
unit.subtitle: Indicative for the known, subjunctive for the unknown

grammar.title: Does the person exist? Let the verb tell us
grammar.intro: In a relative (adjective) clause, the mood of the verb reveals whether the antecedent is real and identified or merely hypothetical, sought, or nonexistent. Compare Busco a alguien que hable ruso (I'm looking for someone — anyone — who speaks Russian) with Conozco a alguien que habla ruso (I know a specific person who does). The difference is entirely in the mood, and it's one of the surest signs of a near-native speaker.

sections.heading: Known antecedent → indicative; unknown → subjunctive
sections.body: If the referent is specific and known to exist, use the indicative. If it's indefinite, hypothetical, or still being searched for, use the subjunctive. The article often signals it: el/la/los/las tends toward the known, un/una/algún toward the unknown.
conj: Conozco a un médico que habla…

ex.en: I have an assistant who knows Chinese.
I need an assistant who knows Chinese.

sections.heading: Negative or nonexistent antecedents
sections.body: When the antecedent is denied or nonexistent — no hay nadie que…, no conozco a nadie que…, no existe… — the subjunctive is obligatory. Note the loss of the personal a with an unknown or negated human referent (Busco alguien / No hay nadie).

ex.es: No hay nadie que sepa tanto como ella.
ex.en: There's no one who knows as much as she does.

ex.es: No conozco a nadie que haya leído todo Cervantes.
ex.en: I don't know anyone who has read all of Cervantes.

sections.heading: Questions, ‘el que / quien’ and open conditions
sections.body: In yes/no questions about existence (¿Hay algún… que…?) the referent is unconfirmed, so use the subjunctive. The same logic drives el que, quien and lo que when they point to an as-yet-unidentified person or thing.

ex.es: ¿Hay algún vuelo que salga antes de las seis?
ex.en: Is there any flight that leaves before six?

ex.es: El que llegue primero que reserve la mesa.
ex.en: Whoever arrives first should book the table.

takeaways: Known, specific antecedent → indicative; indefinite or hypothetical → subjunctive.
Negated or nonexistent antecedents (no hay nadie que…) always take the subjunctive.
Questions about existence (¿Hay algún… que…?) use the subjunctive.
el que / quien / lo que + subjunctive when the referent is not yet identified.

mistakes.w: Busco a una secretaria que habla alemán.
mistakes.r: Busco una secretaria que hable alemán.
mistakes.why: The secretary isn't found yet, so the relative clause needs the subjunctive (hable), and you drop the personal a with an unknown referent.

mistakes.w: No hay nadie que sabe la respuesta.
mistakes.r: No hay nadie que sepa la respuesta.
mistakes.why: A nonexistent antecedent (no hay nadie) forces the subjunctive: sepa, not sabe.
The person's existence is unconfirmed in the question, so use the subjunctive pueda.

exercises.prompt_en: I'm looking for a flat that has a terrace.
exercises.ok: ¡Correcto! El piso aún no existe para ti → subjuntivo.
exercises.no: The flat isn't found yet, so the relative clause takes the subjunctive: “tenga”.

exercises.prompt: Vivo en un piso que ___ una terraza enorme.
exercises.prompt_en: I live in a flat that has a huge terrace.
exercises.ok: ¡Exacto! El piso es real y conocido → indicativo.
exercises.no: This flat is real and specific, so use the indicative: “tiene”.

exercises.prompt: Build: “There's no one who understands me.”
exercises.no: “No hay nadie que me entienda” — a nonexistent antecedent needs the subjunctive entienda.

exercises.prompt_en: Is there anyone here who can speak French?
exercises.hint: Existence is unconfirmed in a question → subjunctive of saber.
exercises.no: The question queries an unconfirmed referent, so use the subjunctive: “sepa”.

exercises.prompt: Match each opening to the correct verb form.
exercises.ok: ¡Excelente! Conocido → indicativo; buscado o inexistente → subjuntivo.

exercises.tts: Necesito un abogado que entienda de fiscalidad.
accepted: necesito un abogado que entienda de fiscalidad
exercises.translation: I need a lawyer who understands taxation.
exercises.ok: ¡Correcto! “Necesito un abogado que entienda de fiscalidad.”
exercises.no: It was: “Necesito un abogado que entienda de fiscalidad.” (I need a lawyer who understands taxation.)

lines.speaker: Elena
lines.es: Para el puesto necesitamos a alguien especial. ¿Tienes a alguien en mente?
lines.en: For the role we need someone special. Do you have anyone in mind?

options.text: Buscamos a alguien que domine tres idiomas y sepa negociar.
Buscamos a alguien que domina tres idiomas y sabe negociar.
Buscamos a alguien que dominara tres idiomas y supiera negociar.

exercises.ok: ¡Perfecto! Perfil aún sin encontrar → presente de subjuntivo.
exercises.no: You're describing an as-yet-unfound profile in the present, so use the present subjunctive: “que domine… y sepa…”.

exercises.say: No conozco a nadie que hable tan rápido.
exercises.en: I don't know anyone who speaks that fast.
exercises.no: Almost — tap “Hear it”, then match the sound of “No conozco a nadie que hable tan rápido.”
